rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention pattern will identify critical pairs and guide window, slope, and temperature refinement.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while holding the window and temperature fixed to test for a faster fully resolved method, using the minimum resolution of 3.98 as headroom.
The six-minute gradient retained maximum CRF with minimum resolution 2.46. Test the next shorter gradient to reduce run time while checking whether the first pair remains above 1.5.

Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary at fixed temperature and solvent window. The first pair may fall below 1.5; the four-minute method remains a fully resolved, maximum-CRF fallback.
At two minutes, only the first pair loses resolution. Test higher temperature at the same slope to probe selectivity changes that could restore this pair while further shortening retention.

Heating worsened the critical separations, so test the lowest temperature at the same two-minute gradient. This isolates the opposite temperature effect and may improve the first pair enough to approach full resolution.

Narrow the gradient window to reduce its slope by about 22%, aiming to raise the first-pair resolution from 1.23 to at least 1.5. The last compound will likely elute during the final hold, so check its retention against the ten-minute scoring threshold.

Shift the solvent window upward while preserving the slope that achieved full resolution in injection 7. The stronger final solvent should shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention; monitor the first pair for any loss from the higher starting organic fraction.

Shift the window upward again at the same slope to accelerate the last peak while targeting the first-pair resolution of 1.59. This tests whether the early pair remains sufficiently retained as the starting organic fraction increases.

Move the constant-slope window up one more grid step to reach the strongest allowed final solvent and shorten late retention. Injection 9 retained full resolution, and its earliest peak was still well beyond the unretained region.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while keeping the strongest final solvent and minimum gradient duration. The shallower slope may improve first-pair resolution while advancing the last peak; check that the earliest peak remains sufficiently retained.

Use the first-pair resolution margin of 1.77 to test a five-degree temperature increase for faster late elution. Keeping the solvent window fixed isolates whether this modest heating preserves full resolution.

Test one higher starting-organic step at the temperature that gave the strongest first-pair separation. This probes the retention boundary for the early peaks while seeking a shorter fully resolved method; injection 12 remains the fastest maximum-CRF fallback.

Return to the starting fraction that preserved early retention and test the next temperature step above injection 12. This brackets the thermal speed–resolution limit; if the first pair drops below 1.5, retain the 30 C method as the fastest fully resolved result.

The higher-temperature and higher-starting-organic tests both compromised the first pair. Reduce the final organic fraction one step from injection 12 to seek more resolution margin with only a modest increase in late retention, while preserving maximum CRF.

Test whether a lower starting fraction and shallower slope restore first-pair resolution at 35 C, where injection 14 failed. This explores a warmer maximum-CRF alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Reduce the gradient span one more step at 35 C to lift the first-pair resolution from 1.42 toward full credit. The last peak may move later during the hold, but its current retention leaves ample margin below ten minutes.

Injection 17 is borderline despite its rounded CRF, so lower temperature to strengthen the critical pair and raise the final organic fraction to accelerate the last peak. This tests a fast alternative to injection 12 with better retention of the earliest peak.

Maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 12 the fastest fully resolved result. Test a four-minute gradient with a lower starting fraction to seek greater separation margin while keeping all peaks comfortably within the ten-minute scoring threshold.

Raise temperature at the four-minute gradient to shorten retention while using injection 19’s first-pair resolution margin of 2.30. This tests a faster, warmer alternative with potential to retain maximum CRF.

Refine around the fastest maximum-CRF methods by combining the lower temperature’s selectivity advantage with a slightly shallower two-minute gradient. This should provide more first-pair resolution margin than injection 12 while keeping the last peak near three minutes.

Test the remaining immediate neighbor of injection 12 by lowering only the starting organic fraction. This checks whether better early retention can preserve full resolution with the strongest final solvent; injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Lower temperature one step from injection 18 to improve its narrow first-pair resolution margin while retaining a short two-minute gradient. This seeks a maximum-CRF alternative with better early retention than injection 12, which remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Narrow the window one step from injection 23 to seek additional first-pair resolution margin while keeping the early peaks retained. The last peak should remain comfortably below ten minutes, preserving maximum CRF if full resolution is maintained.

Raise temperature one step from injection 24 to shorten late retention while targeting enough first-pair resolution to preserve maximum CRF. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with t_last 2.58 minutes.
